- When sentiment is strongly positive (≥ 0.7) and forecast is significantly above recent history, reduce forecast by 5–10% to avoid over-optimism.  
- When sentiment is strongly negative (≤ 0.3) and forecast is below recent history, increase forecast by 5–10% to counteract pessimism.  
- If forecast shows a sharp spike followed by a steep drop, reduce subsequent forecast values by 5–15% to account for overshoot.  
- If forecast mean is consistently higher than true outcome over 3–5 days, apply a 3–5 day mean reversion correction toward historical trend.  
- For 30-day forecasts, if sentiment is volatile (alternating ±0.3 or more), reduce forecast volatility by smoothing with 3-day moving average.  
- If sentiment is high but price is trending downward, adjust forecast to reflect “sentiment vs price divergence” — reduce forecast slope.  
- If forecast is consistently 5–10% above true outcome for 3+ consecutive days, apply downward bias correction of 5–8% for next 3–5 days.  
- If sentiment is low and price is trending upward, reduce forecast by 3–7% to avoid “sentiment lag” misalignment.
